summary: The EQB is a battery-electric version of Mercedes-Benz's boxy GLB small SUV, and its point of difference in Australia is a standard third row in a car under 4.7 metres long. Reviewers are consistent that it rides and insulates like a Mercedes and that the packaging is clever, but equally consistent that the third row is a 5+2 for children, that 100kW DC charging and roughly 350km of real-world range are behind the class in 2026, and that the money buys less car than the badge suggests. It is now a run-out model, with the GLB Electric replacing it locally in the final quarter of 2026.
pros: One of the very few seven-seat EVs on sale here under the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT cap, and the third row is standard on all three variants rather than the $2,900 option it once was
Rides pliantly and quietly even on the standard 20-inch wheels, with sound insulation Australian reviewers rate as a clear step above mainstream electric SUVs
Second row slides through 140mm of travel, so third-row legroom can be traded against boot space rather than being fixed
Compact 4,684mm length and 210mm ground clearance make it far easier to park and garage than a Kia EV9, which needs a $97,000 entry price for the same seat count
Advertised price includes a three-year service plan package and 12 months of Chargefox public charging, which offsets Mercedes-Benz's high standalone servicing costs
cons: Only 130 litres of boot space with all seven seats in use, which CarExpert put behind a Volkswagen Tiguan Allspace in every seating configuration
The third row is explicitly a 5+2: Mercedes-Benz specifies occupants under 1.65m tall, and headroom runs out for adults
DC charging peaks at just 100kW, around half what a Kia EV9 or Tesla Model Y will take, so long-trip stops are noticeably longer
CarExpert measured 19.1kWh/100km in mixed driving against the 536km WLTP claim, cutting realistic range to roughly 350km

Out of production since January 2026 and superseded locally by the GLB Electric in Q4 2026, which leaves resale exposed; at $90,000 the 250+ also has only $1,661 of headroom under the FBT-exemption cap, so one option pack can cost a novated-lease buyer the exemption
